name: Tiji Festival
image_query: Tiji festival Lo Manthang mask dance
when: May, three days in the third Tibetan month (14–16 May in 2026)
summary: Tiji is a three-day festival of masked dances in the main square of Lo Manthang each May, performed by monks of Chhoede Gompa. It retells how the deity Dorje Jono defeated a demon that brought drought to Lo, and ends with the ritual destruction of evil.
body: The name Tiji is usually explained as a shortened form of tenchi, meaning the hope for the Buddha Dharma to prevail. The festival tells the story of Dorje Jono, a form of Vajrakila, who fought his demon father, a creature who caused water shortages and disease in Lo. Over three days the monks of Chhoede Gompa act out the story in elaborate silk costumes and painted masks, accompanied by long horns, drums and cymbals, in the square below the royal palace.

The first day, Tsa Chham, introduces the story with slow, solemn dances; a giant thangka is often displayed on the palace wall. The second day, Nga Chham, brings more dances as Dorje Jono tries to send the demon back to the underworld. On the third day, Rha Chham, the demon is symbolically destroyed, often in the form of a dough effigy, and the procession leaves the walls. Members of the former royal family traditionally attend in formal dress.

Tiji draws people from all over Upper Mustang, many in their best chubas, turquoise and coral jewellery. For visitors it is the best chance to see the walled city at its liveliest, but rooms fill months ahead and jeeps and horses are in high demand. Dates follow the Tibetan calendar: in 2026 the festival fell on 14–16 May. Check the date for your year before you travel.
tips: Book Lo Manthang rooms and Jomsom flights 4–6 months ahead; Tiji is the busiest week of the year.
Arrive at least a day early to acclimatise and find a viewing spot; the square fills fast in the morning.
Do not walk into the dance area or stand in front of the musicians; ask before photographing people and avoid flash.

faqs.a: Tiji is held over three days in the third month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in May. In 2026 it fell on 14–16 May. The 2027 dates are set by the monastery and Tibetan calendar, likely in mid to late May. We confirm dates early in the year; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get to Lo Manthang for Tiji?
faqs.a: Fly Pokhara–Jomsom, then travel to Lo Manthang by jeep in 6–8 hours, usually with a night in Ghami or Tsarang, or trek in 5–6 days from Kagbeni. Some visitors fly by helicopter. All need the Upper Mustang restricted area permit. Plan to arrive at least a day before the festival.

Yes, visitors are welcome to watch the dances in the main square. There is no ticket, but respectful behaviour is expected: stay out of the dance area, do not block locals' view, dress modestly and ask before photographing people. A donation to the monastery is appreciated.

faqs.q: Is a Tiji festival trek worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you plan well. Combining the Upper Mustang trek or jeep tour with Tiji shows Lo Manthang at its most colourful and gives you the region at its best season. The trade-offs are higher prices, crowded lodges and the need to fix your dates around the festival.

name: Yartung Festival
when: August–September, around the full moon of Janai Purnima
summary: Yartung is a summer's-end festival of Mustang, celebrated most famously at Muktinath and in Lo Manthang around the August full moon. It brings horse races, archery, dancing, drinking and pilgrimages, as communities from across the region gather in their finest dress.
body: Yartung, which locals translate as the end of summer, marks the close of the farming season in the high valleys of Mustang. At Muktinath, people from Ranipauwa, Jharkot, Khingar and villages further afield gather near the temple, many on horseback, wearing traditional chubas, felt boots and turquoise jewellery. The celebrations usually coincide with the full moon of Janai Purnima, when Hindu pilgrims also visit Muktinath and Damodar Kunda.

The highlight is horse racing on the open ground near Ranipauwa, with riders galloping decorated horses and showing off tricks. Archery contests, shebru circle dances and plenty of local chhang and rakshi follow. Monks perform rituals at the gompas, and families visit the temple to pray for good harvests and health. The festival lasts around three days, and smaller versions are held in Lo Manthang and other villages.

For visitors, Yartung is a rare chance to see Mustang's horse culture and community life, and it falls in the monsoon, when the rest of Nepal is wet but Muktinath is fairly dry. The catch is travel: Jomsom flights are often disrupted in August and the road from Pokhara has landslides, so build in spare days. Dates change with the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.
tips: Keep two buffer days in your plan for monsoon delays on Jomsom flights or the Beni–Jomsom road.
Stand well back from the race track; horses run fast on rough ground and riders cannot always steer clear.
Join the dances if invited, but go easy on local spirits at 3,700 m.

faqs.a: Yartung is celebrated in August or early September, usually around the full moon of Janai Purnima, for about three days. The exact dates change each year with the lunar calendar and local decisions. We confirm them a few months ahead. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What happens at Yartung festival in Muktinath?
faqs.a: Locals gather near Ranipauwa for horse races, archery, traditional shebru dances, feasting and drinking, and visit the temple and gompas to pray. Riders wear traditional dress and decorate their horses. Hindu pilgrims visit Muktinath at the same time for Janai Purnima, so the area is busy.

Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch the horse races and dances and often get invited to join in. Respect local customs, ask before photographing people and stay clear of the racing ground. Book rooms in Ranipauwa or Jomsom early, as pilgrims and locals fill them.

faqs.q: Is August a good time to visit Muktinath?
faqs.a: It can be. Muktinath lies in a rain shadow and gets little rain, and Yartung and Janai Purnima make it lively. But monsoon cloud often cancels Jomsom flights and landslides block the road from Pokhara. Allow spare days or consider a helicopter, which flies on clear mornings.
